etymology: Hebrew Chakhilah, perhaps “dark” or “drought-stricken”; a hill before Jeshimon in the wilderness of Ziph where David hid from Saul.
biblical_def: Twice the hill of Hachilah is named, and both times it is named by traitors. The Ziphites came up to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Doth not David hide himself with us in strong holds in the wood, in the hill of Hachilah, which is on the south of Jeshimon?” (1Sa 23:19), and again, “Doth not David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah, which is before Jeshimon?” (1Sa 26:1). Here the LORD’s anointed, already sealed with the holy oil by Samuel’s hand, lay hid in a barren place while his own countrymen sold his hiding to the king that sought his life. Hachilah is the hill of the betrayed anointed. It preaches David, but it preaches a greater David, who was likewise betrayed by one of His own, sold for silver, hunted by the rulers of His people, yet all the while kept by His Father’s hand. For upon this very hill God delivered Saul into David’s power, that the anointed who was betrayed might spare the one who hunted him. The saint learns here that the hiding place is not the wood nor the rock, but the LORD Himself, who is round about His people as the mountains are round about Jerusalem. Men may betray the believer’s refuge, but they cannot betray his God.
webster_summary: The hill before Jeshimon where David hid and the Ziphites betrayed his hiding place to Saul (1Sa 23:19); the hill of the betrayed anointed, a figure of Christ betrayed yet kept by His Father.
webster_full: HACHILAH, a hill in the wilderness of Ziph before Jeshimon.
There David hid himself in the strong holds and the wood.
The Ziphites twice betrayed his hiding to Saul (1Sa 23:19; 1Sa 26:1).
Yet upon it the anointed spared the king who hunted him.
A figure of Christ, betrayed by His own yet kept of the Father.
scriptures: Then came up the Ziphites to Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself with us in strong holds in the wood, in the hill of Hachilah, which is on the south of Jeshimon?
And the Ziphites came unto Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah, which is before Jeshimon?
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
Isa 32:2
And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.
corruption_summary: The barren hill where David was betrayed and yet kept; it recovers the truth that the believer’s refuge is the LORD Himself, whom no traitor can betray.
corruption_paragraphs: A desert hill in the wilderness of Ziph provokes no quarrel from the present age; it is passed over in silence, as all such lonely places are. Yet its memory is precious to the church, for here the LORD’s anointed was hunted and betrayed, and here his God did not fail him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the saint’s true hiding place is not any wood or fastness of earth but the living God. Men betrayed the place where David lay, but they could not reach the covenant that kept him. So Christ was betrayed and delivered up, yet kept unto the resurrection; and so His people, though sold and hunted, are hid with Christ in God.
roots_summary: The name Hachilah is joined to a root suggesting darkness or dryness, fitting the barren wilderness of Ziph where it stood.
roots_lines: Hachilah — a hill “on the south” or before Jeshimon (1Sa 23:19).
Jeshimon signifies the waste, the desolate wilderness.
The root is thought to carry the sense of dark or drought-stricken ground.
Twice named, and both times by the betraying Ziphites.
A place of hiding for the hunted anointed of the LORD.
usage: David hid himself in the hill of Hachilah before Jeshimon.
The Ziphites betrayed his hiding place to Saul.
Upon Hachilah the anointed spared the king who sought his life.

etymology: Hebrew Ammah, “a cubit,” hence a measured height or watercourse; the hill before Giah in the wilderness of Gibeon where Joab halted his pursuit of Abner.
biblical_def: When the men of David and the men of Ishbosheth met at the pool of Gibeon, the sword devoured, and Asahel fell by Abner’s spear. Then Joab and Abishai pursued Abner till the light failed: “and the sun went down when they were come to the hill of Ammah, that lieth before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon” (2Sa 2:24). Upon that hill Abner cried out to Joab, Shall the sword devour for ever? and Joab stayed the people, and they pursued no more. The hill of Ammah is the place where the setting sun and a word of restraint together stopped the shedding of a brother’s blood. It is a mournful hill, for it stands in the long and bitter war between the house of Saul and the house of David, kinsmen of one covenant people spending one another’s lives. Yet mercy meets us even here: the LORD sets bounds to civil strife, and He who appoints the going down of the sun appoints also the staying of the sword. The lesson is grave for the household of faith, where brethren too often war as if the sword might devour for ever. Let the sun not go down upon such wrath. The God who is round about His people would have them at peace within their own walls, and He tempers even the fury of kinsmen with the mercy of a set bound.
webster_summary: The hill before Giah where Joab, pursuing Abner, halted as the sun went down (2Sa 2:24); a witness to the mercy that stays the sword among brethren.
webster_full: HILL OF AMMAH, a height before Giah in the wilderness of Gibeon.
Joab and Abishai pursued Abner thither after Asahel’s death.
The sun went down as they came to it (2Sa 2:24).
There Abner asked, Shall the sword devour for ever? and Joab stayed.
A witness that the LORD sets bounds to strife among His people.
scriptures: Joab also and Abishai pursued after Abner: and the sun went down when they were come to the hill of Ammah, that lieth before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon.
And the children of Benjamin gathered themselves together after Abner, and became one troop, and stood on the top of an hill.
And when Joab was come out from David, he sent messengers after Abner, which brought him again from the well of Sirah: but David knew it not.
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
corruption_summary: The hill where the pursuit of Abner was stayed at sundown; it recovers the mercy that sets bounds to strife among brethren.
corruption_paragraphs: This hill in the wilderness of Gibeon draws no fire from the modern mind, being remembered by few; yet the church may not pass it by, for it stands in the sorrowful record of brother warring against brother in the covenant nation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the mercy that stays the sword among brethren. When Abner asked whether the sword should devour for ever, Joab drew back and the pursuit ceased. So within the household of faith let no man’s wrath run on without bound. The setting sun over Ammah preaches the apostle’s word, that we let not the sun go down upon our wrath.
roots_summary: Ammah signifies a cubit or measure, and by extension a channel or aqueduct; a fitting name for a marked height by the wilderness way.
roots_lines: Ammah — from a word meaning a cubit or measure.
Hence also a watercourse or channel, a measured conduit.
The hill lay “before Giah” by the wilderness of Gibeon.
Named once, at the halting of Joab’s pursuit (2Sa 2:24).
A marker of the place where the sword was stayed at sundown.

etymology: Hebrew Gareb, perhaps “scabby” or “leprous,” a common or unclean place; a hill near Jerusalem named in the promise of the city’s restoration.
biblical_def: In the great chapter of the new covenant, where the LORD promises to write His law in the inward parts and to remember sin no more, He adds a word of the city’s rebuilding: “And the measuring line shall yet go forth over against it upon the hill Gareb, and shall compass about to Goath” (Jer 31:39). Gareb bears a name that speaks of scab or leprosy, a mean and unclean spot on the edge of the holy city; yet the measuring line of promise is stretched out over it, and it is drawn within the compass of what shall be holy unto the LORD. The verse following declares that the whole valley, even the place of dead bodies and ashes, shall be holy, and shall not be plucked up nor thrown down any more for ever. Gareb preaches the sanctifying of the common and the cleansing of the unclean. What was scabbed and cast to the outskirts is measured into the city of God. So the covenant of grace takes the leprous sinner, the outcast, the place of ashes, and draws the line of holiness about him, saying he shall not be plucked up any more for ever. Here is the perseverance of the saints written upon a hill: not measured for a season, but compassed into a holiness that abides, a city whose builder and maker is God.
webster_summary: A hill near Jerusalem, its name suggesting the scabbed or unclean, drawn within the measuring line of the promised holy city (Jer 31:39); a figure of the common made holy and kept for ever.
webster_full: HILL OF GAREB, a height near Jerusalem named in Jeremiah’s promise.
Its name suggests the scabbed, leprous, or unclean.
The measuring line of restoration goes forth upon it (Jer 31:39).
It is compassed within what shall be holy unto the LORD.
A figure of the common cleansed and kept, not plucked up for ever.
scriptures: And the measuring line shall yet go forth over against it upon the hill Gareb, and shall compass about to Goath.
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Psa 46:4
There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High.
corruption_summary: An unclean hill drawn into the promised holy city; it recovers the sanctifying grace that makes the common holy and keeps it for ever.
corruption_paragraphs: An obscure hill named once in prophecy stirs no controversy in the present age. What deserves recovery is not a quarrel but a comfort: that the LORD measures the unclean and the outcast into His holy city.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sanctifying grace of the new covenant, which draws the scabbed and common within the compass of holiness and secures it there. The line goes forth upon Gareb, and the word is that nothing shall be plucked up nor thrown down any more for ever. What grace measures in, grace keeps: the outcast becomes the abiding citizen of the city of God.
roots_summary: Gareb is linked to a root meaning scab or itch, hence a leprous or unclean place; the very name magnifies the grace that makes it holy.
roots_lines: Gareb — from a root meaning scab, itch, or leprosy.
Hence a mean or unclean place on the city’s edge.
Named once, in the promise of Jerusalem’s rebuilding (Jer 31:39).
The measuring line is compassed from it about to Goath.
A name of uncleanness swallowed up in a word of holiness.
usage: The measuring line shall go forth upon the hill Gareb.
Gareb was a mean place drawn into the holy city.
From Gareb the line compassed about to Goath.

etymology: Hebrew Gib’ath ha-‘araloth, “the hill of the foreskins” (Jos 5:3), the rise at Gilgal where Joshua circumcised the wilderness generation; the place was thereafter named Gilgal, “rolling,” for the LORD rolled away the reproach of Egypt.
biblical_def: When Israel had passed over Jordan into the land of promise, before ever a wall of Jericho fell, the LORD commanded Joshua to circumcise the people, for the generation born in the wilderness had not been circumcised by the way. So “Joshua made him sharp knives, and circumcised the children of Israel at the hill of the foreskins” (Jos 5:3), and there the LORD said, “This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you” (Jos 5:9). The order is the gospel order: first the sign of the covenant, the cutting away of the flesh, and only then the battle and the inheritance. The land was not won by uncircumcised men trusting their own sword; it was given to a people marked as the LORD’s and made to rest wholly upon His covenant. The hill preaches that the flesh must be cut off before Canaan is entered — not the outward flesh only, for the outward rite was ever a figure of the true. The LORD promised to “circumcise thine heart” (Deu 30:6), and Paul declares the substance: believers are “circumcised with the circumcision made without hands” in Christ (Col 2:11). At Gibeath-haaraloth the reproach of bondage was rolled away and a fresh generation stood consecrated; so in Christ the reproach of sin is rolled away, and the heart, not the flesh, is sealed unto the day of redemption.
webster_summary: The hill at Gilgal where Joshua circumcised the wilderness generation before the conquest, and the LORD rolled away the reproach of Egypt (Jos 5:3-9); a figure of the circumcision of the heart in Christ.
webster_full: GIBEATH-HAARALOTH, the hill of the foreskins, at Gilgal beyond Jordan.
There Joshua circumcised Israel with sharp knives before the conquest (Jos 5:3).
The LORD rolled away the reproach of Egypt and named the place Gilgal (Jos 5:9).
The sign of the covenant went before the battle and the inheritance.
A figure of the circumcision made without hands, the cutting away of the flesh in Christ (Col 2:11).
scriptures: Jos 5:3
And Joshua made him sharp knives, and circumcised the children of Israel at the hill of the foreskins.
Jos 5:9
And the LORD said unto Joshua, This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you. Wherefore the name of the place is called Gilgal unto this day.
Deu 30:6
And the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart, and the heart of thy seed, to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live.
Col 2:11
In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ:
corruption_summary: The hill where the covenant sign preceded the conquest; it recovers the truth that the flesh must be cut off and the heart circumcised in Christ before the soul enters its rest.
corruption_paragraphs: The abiding lesson of Gibeath-haaraloth is that God deals with His people by covenant, and that the sign of the covenant is no empty ceremony but a summons to the reality it signifies. Israel could not take the land as a people careless of the LORD’s mark upon them; the rite went before the war. So the outward sign, whether the circumcision of old or baptism now, is honoured as God’s appointed token, yet it is never mistaken for the inward grace, which is the circumcision of the heart wrought by the Spirit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A hill named for a forgotten rite raises no modern quarrel. The principle to recover is that the reproach of our old bondage is rolled away not by our striving but by the LORD, and that He seals His people inwardly — “circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter” (Rom 2:29) — before He leads them on to their inheritance.
roots_summary: From gib’ah, a hill, and ‘orlah, foreskin; the compound marks the place of Israel’s circumcision, renamed Gilgal from galal, to roll.
roots_lines: Gib’ah — a hill, height, or rising ground.
‘Orlah — foreskin; also used of the “uncircumcised” heart, ear, and lips.
Gilgal, from galal (to roll), names the same place: the reproach “rolled away.”
The uncircumcised (‘arel) is the covenant outsider; the circumcised, the marked people of God.
The New Testament fulfils the figure in peritome acheiropoietos, circumcision made without hands (Col 2:11).
usage: At Gibeath-haaraloth the covenant sign was renewed before a blow was struck against Jericho.
The naming of the hill teaches that God rolls away the reproach of His people by His own hand.
As Israel was circumcised at the hill before the conquest, so the heart is circumcised in Christ before the soul enters its rest.

etymology: Hebrew Amanah, “faithful” or “sure,” from a root meaning to be firm; a peak of the Anti-Lebanon whence the Bridegroom calls His spouse.
biblical_def: In the Song, the Bridegroom calls His bride away from the perilous heights: “Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions’ dens, from the mountains of the leopards” (Son 4:8). Amana is a summit of the Anti-Lebanon, its very name signifying faithfulness and firmness, a mountain of danger where lions couch and leopards range. The voice is the voice of Christ, the true Bridegroom, calling His church down from the mountains of peril to Himself. He does not leave her among the lions’ dens; He bids her look away from Amana and come with Him. Twice He says “with me,” for it is not merely from the danger but unto His person that He calls her. The name Amana preaches what the summons secures: the faithful, firm, covenant love of the Bridegroom, who will not lose His spouse to the beasts of the mountains. And still His Spirit and His bride say, Come; and to every soul yet lodged among the leopards He calls, Come with me. The church has no safety upon the heights of her own attainment or her own danger, but only in going down to Christ at His word. From the top of Amana He calls her home to the faithfulness that His own name upholds.
webster_summary: A peak of the Anti-Lebanon, its name signifying faithfulness, whence the Bridegroom calls His spouse from the lions’ dens (Son 4:8); a figure of Christ calling His church from danger to Himself.
webster_full: AMANA, a summit of Lebanon named in the Song of Solomon.
Its name signifies faithful, firm, or sure.
Thence the Bridegroom calls His spouse to come (Son 4:8).
It stands among the lions’ dens and mountains of leopards.
A figure of Christ calling His church from danger unto Himself.
scriptures: Son 4:8
Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards.
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
A Song of degrees. I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
corruption_summary: The mountain of danger from which the Bridegroom calls His bride; it recovers the reading of the Song as the espousal love of Christ and His church.
corruption_paragraphs: A mountain-top named in the Song raises no dispute with the present age, save that the age has largely forgotten to read the Song as the love of Christ and His church. The recovery needed is that older and truer reading.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the espousal love of Christ for His church, that He calls her by name from the mountains of danger to Himself. The Song is no mere earthly ballad but the marriage-song of the Lamb and His bride. From the top of Amana the Bridegroom cries, Come with me; and the faithfulness His name declares is the ground of the church’s safety.
roots_summary: Amana springs from the root aman, to be firm, faithful, sure — the same root that gives us Amen; the mountain of danger bears a name of faithfulness.
roots_lines: Amana — from aman, to be firm, faithful, sure.
The same root yields the word Amen.
Named with Shenir and Hermon as a Lebanon height (Son 4:8).
A place of lions’ dens and mountains of leopards.
A name of faithfulness set upon a mountain of peril.
usage: Look from the top of Amana, saith the Bridegroom.
Amana signifies faithful or sure.
Christ calls His spouse from Amana to Himself.

etymology: Hebrew Moreh, “teacher” or “instruction,” from a root to teach or point out; the plain or oak of Moreh at Shechem where Abram built his first altar in Canaan. Distinct from the hill of Moreh in the vale of Jezreel.
biblical_def: When Abram first entered the land of promise, he came to Shechem: “And Abram passed through the land unto the place of Sichem, unto the plain of Moreh. And the Canaanite was then in the land” (Gen 12:6). At this plain, or oak, of Moreh — a name that speaks of teaching — the LORD appeared to him and said, Unto thy seed will I give this land; and there Abram built his first altar unto the LORD who had appeared to him. It is worth marking the words that stand beside the altar: “the Canaanite was then in the land.” Abram raised his worship in the midst of enemy territory, upon no possession of his own, on the bare word of promise alone. He had not one foot of the land in hand, yet he built an altar and called upon the name of the LORD. Here is the first altar of the pilgrim faith. It teaches that true worship rests not upon the believer’s present possession but upon God’s promise; that the saint may set up the worship of God in the very country of his foes; and that faith takes God at His word before it sees the inheritance. Moreh signifies instruction, and this oak instructs the church still: build your altar on the promise, though the Canaanite be in the land. This is not the hill of Moreh in Jezreel where Gideon camped, but the oak of Abram’s first worship.
webster_summary: The plain or oak of Moreh at Shechem where Abram built his first altar in Canaan though the Canaanite was in the land (Gen 12:6); the first altar of the pilgrim faith. Distinct from the hill of Moreh in Jezreel.
webster_full: OAK OF MOREH, the plain of Moreh at Shechem in Canaan.
The name signifies teaching or instruction.
There Abram built his first altar to the LORD (Gen 12:6).
He worshipped though the Canaanite was then in the land.
Distinct from the hill of Moreh in the vale of Jezreel.

Are they not on the other side Jordan, by the way where the sun goeth down, in the land of the Canaanites, which dwell in the champaign over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh?
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
corruption_summary: The oak of Abram’s first altar at Shechem; it recovers the boldness of the pilgrim faith that worships on the promise even in the enemy’s land.
corruption_paragraphs: The plain of Moreh is chiefly confused, not corrupted — taken for the hill of Moreh in Jezreel where Gideon encamped. This entry attends the Genesis oak of Abram’s first altar, a different place bearing the same name of instruction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the boldness of the pilgrim faith, which builds its altar upon the promise of God even where the enemy holds the land. Abram possessed nothing but the word, yet he worshipped. So the church, a stranger and pilgrim in a world not yet subdued to Christ, sets up the pure worship of God on the ground of promise, waiting for the inheritance sure to come.
roots_summary: Moreh comes from yarah, to throw, point out, or teach; hence Moreh means teacher or instruction, and this oak of Moreh is the place of teaching.
roots_lines: Moreh — from yarah, to point out or teach.
Hence Moreh signifies teacher or instruction.
Rendered plain or oak of Moreh at Shechem (Gen 12:6).
Named again as a landmark of the covenant charge (Deu 11:30).
Not the hill of Moreh in Jezreel of Judges 7.
usage: Abram built his first altar at the plain of Moreh.

etymology: Hebrew Charod, “trembling” or “terror,” from a root to tremble; the well beside which Gideon’s army was winnowed to three hundred.
biblical_def: Beside the well of Harod, whose name means trembling, the LORD reduced an army. “Then Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, and all the people that were with him, rose up early, and pitched beside the well of Harod: so that the host of the Midianites were on the north side of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley” (Jdg 7:1). Two and thirty thousand had gathered; but the LORD said, The people are yet too many, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me. So the fearful were sent home, and the rest were tried by the water of that trembling well: the three hundred that lapped, putting the hand to the mouth, were kept, and by them alone the LORD broke Midian. Harod is the well of winnowing, where self-confidence is poured out like water and only the little remnant is left. The place teaches the sovereign method of salvation: the LORD saves by the few, or by the one, that no flesh should glory in His presence and that the whole praise should be His alone. It is the doctrine of grace written in a battle. God will not share His glory with the arm of man; He chooses the weak things and the base things and the things which are not, to bring to nought the things that are. Let the church learn at Harod to distrust her numbers and her strength, and to trust the LORD who saves by three hundred as easily as by ten thousand.
webster_summary: The well where the LORD winnowed Gideon’s army to three hundred, lest Israel vaunt themselves (Jdg 7:1); the well of trembling where self-confidence is poured out that the glory may be God’s alone.
webster_full: HAROD, a well in the valley by the hill of Moreh.
Its name signifies trembling or terror.
There Gideon’s host was winnowed to three hundred (Jdg 7:1).
The LORD saved by the few, lest Israel vaunt themselves.
A witness that God will not share His glory with man.
scriptures: Jdg 7:1

Then Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, and all the people that were with him, rose up early, and pitched beside the well of Harod: so that the host of the Midianites were on the north side of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.
Psa 83:9
Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison:
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.

corruption_summary: The well where Gideon’s army was thinned to three hundred; it recovers the sovereign truth that the LORD saves by the few, that the glory may be His alone.
corruption_paragraphs: The well of Harod occasions no modern redefinition; the story of Gideon’s three hundred is well loved, but its point is often mislaid, made a tale of heroism rather than of divine sovereignty.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD saves by the few that the glory may be His alone. He thinned the army on purpose, lest Israel say, Mine own hand hath saved me. The battle of Harod is the doctrine of grace in arms: God chooses the weak and the small, and gives victory, that no flesh should glory in His presence but the whole praise return to Him.
roots_summary: Harod is from charad, to tremble or be afraid; the well of trembling, fitly named where the fearful were sifted out and the mighty host reduced.
roots_lines: Harod — from charad, to tremble or be terrified.
Hence the well of trembling or of fear.
There the fearful of Israel were sent home.
The three hundred were chosen by the manner of their drinking (Jdg 7:1).
The Midianites lay northward, by the hill of Moreh.
usage: Gideon pitched beside the well of Harod.
At Harod the army was winnowed to three hundred.
Harod signifies trembling or terror.

etymology: Hebrew Misrephoth Mayim, “burnings of waters,” perhaps salt-pits or hot springs; the far northern point to which Israel chased the routed northern kings.
biblical_def: When Jabin king of Hazor gathered the kings of the north with horses and chariots very many, a host like the sand upon the sea shore, the LORD delivered them into Israel’s hand: “who smote them, and chased them unto great Zidon, and unto Misrephothmaim, and unto the valley of Mizpeh eastward; and they smote them, until they left them none remaining” (Jos 11:8). Misrephoth-maim, the burnings of waters, marks the utmost bound of the pursuit — the far edge to which the enemy was driven and beyond which none escaped. The word that crowns the verse is the word to lay hold of: “they left them none remaining.” The LORD’s victory over the great coalition of Canaan was not partial but complete; the chase did not slacken until the field was cleared. Herein is a figure of the thoroughness of grace against sin. The LORD does not half-save nor leave the enemy a foothold in His people; what He undertakes to subdue, He subdues to the uttermost. The saint is not to make peace with a remnant of his corruptions, sparing an Agag, leaving some Canaanite in the land; he is to pursue sin unto Misrephoth-maim, unto the burnings of waters, and leave it none remaining. For Christ our Joshua will at length put all enemies under His feet, and destroy the last enemy, and leave death itself none remaining.
webster_summary: The far northern point to which Israel chased and utterly smote Jabin’s coalition, leaving none remaining (Jos 11:8); a figure of the completeness of the LORD’s victory and the thoroughness of grace against sin.
webster_full: MISREPHOTH-MAIM, a far northern point by great Zidon.
The name signifies burnings of waters, perhaps salt-pits.
Israel chased the northern kings thither (Jos 11:8).
They smote them until they left them none remaining.
A figure of the LORD’s complete victory over His enemies.
scriptures: Jos 11:8

And the LORD delivered them into the hand of Israel, who smote them, and chased them unto great Zidon, and unto Misrephothmaim, and unto the valley of Mizpeh eastward; and they smote them, until they left them none remaining.

corruption_summary: The far bound of Israel’s northern conquest, where the enemy was left none remaining; it recovers the completeness of the LORD’s victory and the thoroughness of grace against sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This remote place-name provokes no present-day quarrel. What the church must recover from the verse is the completeness of the LORD’s conquest, a truth easily softened in an age loath to speak of the utter overthrow of evil.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the thoroughness of grace against sin. The LORD left the enemies of His people none remaining, and He will not leave His saints half-delivered. Let none spare a favourite corruption or a surviving Agag, but pursue sin to the uttermost, as Israel chased the foe unto Misrephoth-maim; for Christ shall put all enemies under His feet and leave the last enemy none remaining.

etymology: Hebrew Shepher, “beauty” or “goodliness,” from a root to be fair; a wilderness encampment of Israel between Kehelathah and Haradah.
biblical_def: Among the forty-two stages that Moses set down of Israel’s wandering, one bears a lovely name: “And they went from Kehelathah, and pitched in mount Shapher” (Num 33:23), and again, “And they removed from mount Shapher, and encamped in Haradah” (Num 33:24). Shapher signifies beauty, goodliness, fairness — a mount of beauty in the midst of a great and terrible wilderness of drought and fiery serpents. It is easy to pass such a name unregarded, a single camp between two others in a barren list; yet the Spirit troubled to record it, and its very name preaches. There is beauty even in the desert stages of the pilgrimage. The way to Canaan lay through the waste, but the LORD set a mount of goodliness in it, and He orders every camp of His people, whether the name be beauty or trembling, according to His wisdom and His mercy. No stage is wasted; no barren mile is unnumbered. The saint travelling through the wilderness of this world may look for the mounts of Shapher that his God appoints — the fair providences, the sweet ordinances, the seasons of refreshing that break the drought. And he may trust that even the barren stages between are ordered by the same hand that pitched him at the mount of beauty. The desert is His, and He makes it, in His own places and times, to bud and blossom as the rose.
webster_summary: A wilderness encampment between Kehelathah and Haradah, its name meaning beauty or goodliness (Num 33:23); a mount of fairness in the desert, teaching that the LORD orders every stage of the pilgrimage.

corruption_paragraphs: A lone encampment in the wilderness itinerary faces no modern redefinition. Its use is devotional: to teach that no stage of the believer’s pilgrimage, however obscure, falls outside the ordering care of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God over every step of the pilgrim way. He set a mount of beauty in the desert and numbered the camp, that His people might know no barren mile is unregarded. The wilderness stages of the Christian life are appointed by the same hand; and the saint may look for the fair providences his God has set even in the driest country.

etymology: Hebrew Rimmon Perets, “pomegranate of the breach”; a wilderness station of Israel between Rithmah and Libnah in the forty years’ wandering.
biblical_def: In the register of Israel’s journeyings the eye passes a station easily overlooked: “And they departed from Rithmah, and pitched at Rimmonparez” (Num 33:19), and then, “And they departed from Rimmonparez, and pitched in Libnah” (Num 33:20). The name signifies the pomegranate of the breach, and it is neither the town of Rimmon in the south nor the rock Rimmon whither Benjamin fled, but a distinct camp of the forty years’ wandering. Why did the Spirit record such names, camp by camp, breach by breach, through the long desert? That the church might read the faithfulness of God written in an itinerary. He counted every camp of His people; He led them by the way, He knew their down-sitting and their uprising, and not one station of their wandering fell from His remembrance. The barren list is a monument of covenant faithfulness: the God who fed them with manna and led them through that great and terrible wilderness kept the tally of every stage, that His mercy might be told to the generations. So the believer’s life, though it seem a wandering from one obscure camp to another, is numbered by his God. The stations that no man remembers are remembered by the LORD; He who pitched Israel at Rimmon-parez pitches His pilgrim people still, and will bring them at the last through every breach to the land of rest.
webster_summary: A wilderness station between Rithmah and Libnah in the forty years’ wandering (Num 33:19), distinct from the town and the rock of Rimmon; a witness to the God who counted every camp of His people.

corruption_paragraphs: This obscure station is chiefly liable to confusion with the town of Rimmon and the rock Rimmon whither Benjamin fled, not to any modern redefinition. This entry attests it a distinct camp of the wilderness itinerary.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant faithfulness of God, who wrote down every stage of His people’s wandering. The barren list of camps is a record of mercy: He led them, He numbered them, He forgot none of them. So the pilgrim may trust that his own obscure and wandering way is remembered by the LORD, who will bring him through every breach to the land of promised rest.
